sentences: The government may raise fuel taxes.
Then fewer people will drive.
drills.hint: Use the present simple after "if" and "will" in the main clause.

sentences: Students might revise every day.
Then they will do better in exams.
drills.hint: No comma is needed when "if" comes in the middle of the sentence.

sentences: Cities may plant more trees.
Then the air will be cleaner.
drills.hint: Put a comma after the "if" clause when it starts the sentence.

sentences: Employees may get flexible hours.
Then they will feel less stressed.
drills.hint: The condition comes after "if"; the result uses "will".

sentences: Children may eat too much sugar.
Then they will damage their teeth.
drills.hint: After "if", use the present simple even though the meaning is future.

sentences: More tourists may visit the island.
Then local businesses will earn more.
drills.hint: The result can come first; then "if" introduces the condition.

sentences: People may recycle their plastic bottles.
Then less waste will go to landfill.
drills.hint: Start with the condition, add a comma, then give the result with "will".

sentences: More people may work from home.
Then city roads will be quieter.
drills.hint: Do not use "will" in the "if" clause, even for a future idea.

sentences: Hospitals may hire more nurses.
Then patients will wait less.
drills.hint: Give the result first, then add "if" + present simple.

sentences: You may read English news daily.
Then your vocabulary will grow quickly.
drills.hint: "If" + present simple gives a real future possibility.

sentences: Food prices may continue to rise.
Then poorer families will struggle.
drills.hint: Use the present simple, not "will", in the "if" clause.

sentences: A city may build a new metro line.
Then traffic jams will decrease.
drills.hint: Use a third-person "-s" verb after "if" with a singular subject.

sentences: Young people may not exercise.
Then they will face health problems later.
drills.hint: A negative condition after "if" still uses the present simple.

sentences: Suppose public transport were free.
Far fewer people would drive.
drills.hint: For an unreal situation, use the past after "if" and "would" in the result.

sentences: Suppose every school had a garden.
Children would learn more about food.
drills.hint: Second conditional: "would" in the result and past simple after "if".

sentences: Suppose I had more free time.
I would learn a new language.
drills.hint: Use the past simple after "if" for an imaginary situation.

sentences: Suppose cars were banned from city centres.
Streets would be safer for cyclists.
drills.hint: A passive verb in the past works after "if" in a second conditional.

sentences: Suppose governments taxed sugary drinks heavily.
People would consume less sugar.
drills.hint: Match "would" in the result with a past verb after "if".

sentences: Suppose housing were cheaper.
More young people would buy homes.
drills.hint: Use "were" after "if" for an imaginary present situation.

sentences: Suppose all workers earned a fair wage.
Fewer people would live in poverty.
drills.hint: An imaginary condition takes a past verb; the result takes "would".

sentences: Suppose scientists found a cure for ageing.
The world population would grow rapidly.
drills.hint: In a second conditional the result needs "would", not "will".

sentences: Suppose museums were open at night.
More office workers would visit them.
drills.hint: The "if" clause can come second; then no comma is needed.

sentences: Suppose every student had a laptop.
Online learning would be easier.
drills.hint: Imaginary present: "if" + past simple, then "would" + verb.

sentences: Suppose companies did not advertise to children.
Children would ask for fewer toys.
drills.hint: A negative unreal condition uses "did not" after "if".

sentences: Suppose farmers used fewer chemicals.
Rivers would be much cleaner.
drills.hint: Use the past simple after "if" and "would be" for the imagined result.

sentences: Governments may not act soon.
Then climate change will get worse.
drills.hint: "Unless" means "if ... not", so the verb after it is positive.

sentences: Patients may not finish their medicine.
Then the infection will return.
drills.hint: Put "unless" before the condition; use a positive verb after it.

sentences: Small shops may not go online.
Then many will close within a few years.
drills.hint: A fronted "unless" clause needs a comma before the main clause.

sentences: Teenagers may not get enough sleep.
Then they will get lower grades.
drills.hint: "Unless" + present simple describes a future risk.

sentences: Cities may not invest in flood defences.
Then coastal areas will be at risk.
drills.hint: Never use "not" after "unless"; it already means "if not".

sentences: Tourists may not respect local customs.
Then they will cause offence.
drills.hint: "Unless" introduces what must happen to avoid the result.

sentences: Children may not learn to swim.
Then they will be in danger near water.
drills.hint: Begin with "unless" + positive verb, then a comma and the result.

sentences: The company may not cut its costs.
Then it will lose money this year.
drills.hint: Use the present simple after "unless" for a future condition.

sentences: Wild animals may not be protected.
Then many species will disappear.
drills.hint: A passive verb can follow "unless": "unless" + be + past participle.

sentences: Workers may not wear helmets.
Then they will not be allowed on site.
answer: will not be allowed on site
drills.hint: The main clause can be negative; the "unless" clause stays positive.

sentences: Prices may not fall.
Then fewer people will travel abroad.
drills.hint: "Unless" + present simple; "will" belongs only in the main clause.

sentences: Students can use phones in class.
They must use them for research.
drills.hint: "Provided that" introduces a condition that must be met.

sentences: The project will succeed.
It must receive enough funding.
drills.hint: When "provided that" starts the sentence, add a comma after the condition.

sentences: Remote work can be productive.
Staff must have clear goals.
drills.hint: Put the main idea first, then "provided that" + subject + verb.

sentences: Tourism can help rural areas.
It must be managed carefully.
drills.hint: A passive verb can follow "provided that".

sentences: Older drivers can keep their licences.
They must pass a regular eye test.
drills.hint: Use the present simple after "provided that", not "will".

sentences: Anyone can join the sports club.
They must pay a small fee.
drills.hint: "Provided that" is followed by a full clause, not a noun alone.

sentences: Fast food is acceptable occasionally.
It must be part of a balanced diet.
drills.hint: "Provided that" means "only on this condition".

sentences: The new stadium will create jobs.
It must be completed on time.
drills.hint: Fronted condition, comma, then the result with "will".

sentences: Social media can be useful for learning.
Users must check their sources.
drills.hint: "Provided that" + present simple shows a necessary condition.

sentences: Elderly people can live independently.
They must receive regular support.
drills.hint: Keep the verb after "provided that" in the present simple.

sentences: Visitors can enter the gallery for free.
They must book online first.
answer: can enter the gallery for free
drills.hint: "Providing that" works like "provided that": it gives a condition.

sentences: The economy will grow next year.
Exports must remain strong.
drills.hint: Start with the condition and put a comma before the main clause.

sentences: Pets are allowed in the flats.
They must not disturb the neighbours.
drills.hint: A negative condition after "providing that" uses "do not" + verb.

sentences: Homework can improve learning.
It must not take too long.
drills.hint: Use "does not" with a singular subject after "providing that".

sentences: Electric cars will become popular.
Charging points must be widely available.
drills.hint: Do not put "will" after "providing that"; use the present simple.

sentences: Teenagers can work part-time.
Their studies must not suffer.
drills.hint: The condition after "providing that" has its own subject and verb.

sentences: Street markets can attract tourists.
They must be kept clean.
drills.hint: "Providing that" links a possible result to the condition it needs.

sentences: The festival will go ahead.
The weather must stay dry.
drills.hint: Use the present simple after "providing that" for a future condition.

sentences: Exercise is good for you.
You must not overdo it.
drills.hint: "As long as" means "only if"; it is followed by a clause.

sentences: Children can watch television.
They must finish their homework first.
drills.hint: Put the permission first, then "as long as" + the condition.

sentences: Prices will stay low.
Supply must remain high.
drills.hint: A fronted "as long as" clause is followed by a comma.

sentences: Online courses can work well.
Students must stay motivated.
drills.hint: No comma is needed when "as long as" comes in the middle.

sentences: Rural areas may continue to offer few jobs.
Then cities will keep growing.
drills.hint: "As long as" can mean "for the whole time that"; use the present simple.

sentences: Workers will stay loyal.
They must feel valued.
drills.hint: Give the result first, then the condition after "as long as".

sentences: Commercial fishing can continue.
Fish stocks must stay healthy.
drills.hint: "As long as" + subject + present simple verb.

sentences: The team will win the league.
Its best players must stay fit.
drills.hint: Never use "will" straight after "as long as".

sentences: Families can save money.
They must plan their spending.
drills.hint: Begin with the condition, then a comma and the possible result.

sentences: The bank lent the firm money.
The firm had to repay the loan within a year.
drills.hint: "On condition that" sets a strict condition; keep both verbs in the past.

sentences: The student was given a scholarship.
She had to keep high grades.
drills.hint: "On condition that" is followed by a full clause.

sentences: The council approved the new hotel.
It had to include green spaces.
drills.hint: Use a past verb after "on condition that" when the story is in the past.

sentences: Researchers may use the data.
They must protect people's privacy.
drills.hint: After "on condition that", use the present simple, not "will".

sentences: The factory can stay open.
It must reduce its pollution.
drills.hint: "On condition that" is a formal way to state a requirement.

sentences: The athlete can compete again.
He must pass a fitness test.
drills.hint: Use a third-person "-s" verb after "on condition that" here.

sentences: The landlord agreed to lower the rent.
The tenants had to sign a longer contract.
drills.hint: The condition explains what the other person had to do in return.

sentences: The film can be shown in schools.
Some scenes must be removed.
drills.hint: A passive verb can follow "on condition that".

sentences: Hikers should carry extra water.
They might get lost.
drills.hint: "In case" shows a precaution: act now because something might happen.

sentences: Save your essay regularly.
Your computer might crash.
drills.hint: "In case" + subject + present simple; "in case of" needs a noun.

sentences: Many families keep some savings.
They might lose their jobs.
drills.hint: The action is a precaution; "in case" gives the possible problem.

sentences: Coastal towns build sea walls.
Storms might cause flooding.
drills.hint: "In case" introduces a risk, not a purpose or a result.

sentences: Travellers should buy insurance.
They might fall ill abroad.
drills.hint: After "in case", use the present simple, not "will".

sentences: Schools practise fire drills.
A real fire might break out.
drills.hint: "In case" explains why people prepare for something possible.

sentences: Hospitals store extra blood.
There might be a major accident.
drills.hint: "In case" is a precaution, not "if": the action happens anyway.

sentences: Visitors should bring a coat.
It might get cold in the evening.
drills.hint: Use "in case" + a clause to give the reason for a precaution.

sentences: Scientists keep copies of their data.
The originals might be damaged.
drills.hint: "In case" can be followed by a passive clause.

sentences: The exam may be difficult.
Well-prepared students will still pass.
drills.hint: "Even if" means the result stays the same whatever happens.

sentences: Students may fail the test.
They can still retake it.
drills.hint: Put the result first; "even if" adds a condition that changes nothing.

sentences: The factory may close.
Most workers will find new jobs.
drills.hint: Use the present simple after "even if" and "will" in the main clause.

sentences: Online shopping may grow further.
Many people will still visit local markets.
drills.hint: No "will" after "even if"; use the present simple.

sentences: The library may close early.
Students can still study online.
drills.hint: "Even if" + clause; "still" in the main clause shows no change.

sentences: Suppose tuition were free.
Some young people would still not go to university.
drills.hint: "Even if" can take a past verb and "would" for imaginary situations.

sentences: A diet may be healthy.
It will not work without exercise.
drills.hint: Begin with "even if", add a comma, then the unchanged result.

sentences: Housing may get cheaper.
Young people will still struggle to save.
drills.hint: "Even if" is followed by a subject and verb, unlike "despite".

sentences: Cities must reduce traffic.
If not, air quality will get worse.
drills.hint: Use a semicolon before "otherwise" and a comma after it.

sentences: Students should start their essays early.
If not, they will run out of time.
drills.hint: "Otherwise" means "if not"; it introduces the bad result.

sentences: Farmers need more rain.
If not, the crops will fail.
drills.hint: "Otherwise" shows what will happen if the first idea does not happen.

sentences: Old buildings must be repaired.
Without this, they may collapse.
drills.hint: "Otherwise" joins two full clauses, so a semicolon comes before it.

sentences: Shoppers should compare prices.
If not, they may pay too much.
drills.hint: Give the advice first, then "otherwise" + the possible problem.

sentences: Companies must train their staff.
If not, they will lose customers.
drills.hint: "Otherwise" means "if not", not "so"; check the meaning carefully.

sentences: Patients should follow medical advice.
If not, they may recover slowly.
drills.hint: The first clause gives the advice; "otherwise" warns of the risk.

sentences: Endangered species need protection.
Without it, they may die out.
drills.hint: Put a semicolon before "otherwise" and a comma straight after it.

sentences: Recycling schemes work well.
People must sort their waste correctly.
drills.hint: "Only if" shows that this is the one condition needed.

sentences: Bans on plastic bags succeed.
Shops must offer cheap alternatives.
drills.hint: "Only if" stresses a necessary condition; "even if" means the opposite.

sentences: Students can enter the exam hall.
They must show their ID cards.
drills.hint: Put "only if" before the single condition that allows the action.

sentences: Tourism benefits local people.
Profits must stay in the community.
drills.hint: "Only if" + present simple: without this condition, the result fails.
